Project_Description: Through funding from NOAA’s Restoration Center, in partnership with the US Fish and Wildlife Foundation, the Pinellas County Environmental Foundation, and others, volunteers constructed a bridge to restore circulation to the back bays of Mullet Key in Ft. DeSoto Park, Florida. Tidal flow between bays in the Fort DeSoto Park Aquatic Habitat Management Area in Pinellas County were severed during the dredging and filling activities that occurred in the late 1950s.  Summertime temperatures become extremely elevated in these areas leading to very low dissolved oxygen levels as well as severe seagrass stress. Restored circulation has improved water quality healthier essential fish habitat. Fish and crabs had migrated into the area within a few days.

Habitat_Description: Highlands Hammock State Park (9,251 acres) is managed by the Florida Department of Environmental Protection and is located in eastern Hardee and western Highlands Counties near the Highlands Ridge. A mosaic of 15 natural upland and wetland habitats occur in the park including mesic flatwoods, sand hill, scrub, scrubby flatwoods, depression marsh and cypress, as well as ruderal and developed lands. Native vegetation includes saw palmetto, slash pine, longleaf pine, cypress, several species of oak, hooded pitcher plant, gall berry, blueberries, and tarflower. There are several freshwater creeks including Tiger Creek and Haw Branch. The habitats support a great diversity of wildlife, birds and fish including scrub jay, swallow tail kite, snail kite, alligators, Florida black bear, Florida panther and bob cat. The pine flatwoods have heavy fire fuel loads and there are high numbers of feral hogs, and extensive areas of invasive exotic vegetation including soda apple, bamboo, Guinea grass, ginger lily, climbing fern, air potato and cogongrass. The park is managed for habitat protection and restoration, as well as public access and recreation, focusing on hiking.

Project_Name: Indian River Lagoon Habitat Restoration - Bee Gum Point (IR Land Trust)
Project_Description:
This entry is one of 10 project sites included under the name "Indian River Lagoon Habitat Restoration". 

The Indian River Lagoon Council will implement a large-scale restoration in response to an urgent need to restore essential fish habitats, enhance ecosystem functions, and increase resilience in the Indian River Lagoon (IRL) on the Atlantic Coast of Florida.  The overall project design integrates a multi-habitat and multi-site restoration approach that recognizes the complex spatial and temporal diversity of the IRL. The overall project includes a network of 10 discrete project sites and 15 individual projects that cumulatively include restoration and/or enhancement of  seagrass (46 acres), oyster (6.5 acres), saltmarsh wetland (2,125 acres), and living shoreline (6,045 linear feet) habitats.  The project will also re-introduce native clams (21 million) to enhance seagrass habitat.  The ten individual projects will engage the community through site specific outreach events and volunteer opportunities.  

This project in the central IRL will enhance 125 acres of impounded wetlands and 10 acres of seagrass habitat through the installation of two culverts.  The project will also  enhance a living shoreline through mangrove plantings and will deploy Spartan Fish Reefs to enhance essential fish habitat along the shoreline.  Volunteer opportunities will be created through the Indian River Land Trust and fishing opportunities will be improved for local subsistence fishers.

Project_Description: The St. John River Water Management District worked with the Brevard County Mosquito Control District and the Merritt Island National Wildlife Refuge to install culverts to enhance fish habitat in Brevard County, FL.  At the Sykes Creek Impoundments (C-2 North and C-2 South), which comprise nearly 2,015 acres of wetland, 17 culverts were installed to recreate flow where natural creek mouths previously existed and provide fish with access to habitat.  Work began on this component in September of 2015, restoring 1,289 acres.  The balance of acreage was completed in the fall of 2015.  Additional work is being implemented in other impoundments within the Merritt Island National Wildlife Refuge to address subsidence. Subsidence has reduced sediment levels to elevations too low to support marsh grass or mangrove habitat.  This component of the project was implemented first as a pilot project to evaluate a variety of methods to bring subsided areas up to an appropriate elevation to support vegetation typical of wetlands in the area. Project_Description: The goal of Tampa Bay Watch’s Community Oyster Reef Enhancement program is to increase oyster populations in Tampa Bay while improving water quality, reducing erosion, promoting fish and wildlife habitats, and increasing coastal resilience. Project_Name: Mulberry Mangrove/Tidal Creek Project and Lewis Lake Project
Project_Description: On December 7, 1997, over 50 million gallons of acidic process water was released into the Alafia River from a fertilizer plant in Mulberry, Polk County, Florida. The release injured natural resources in the Alafia River and in Tampa Bay. Several public agencies, including NOAA, FDEP and EPC, worked together to assess natural resource injuries and losses caused by the Spill and to recover natural resource damages to compensate for these losses from the party responsible. This project consisted of two components implemented on MacDill Airforce Base: the Mangrove/Tidal Creek project and the Lewis Lake Project.  The first component involved the restoration of 34 acres of intertidal lagoons/channels, high and low marsh platforms, mangrove islands, upland islands, upland hammocks, and relic mangrove forest. To accomplish project goals, large stands of non-native vegetation had to be removed, followed by excavation of lagoons and channels to restore tidal availability. The second component, the Lewis Lake Project, modified an existing freshwater/oligohaline stormwater treatment pond that was intermittently intertidal via the pond’s overflow control structure. This 26.6 acre project increased the size of the pond, created new open water and marsh platforms, removed all cattails and other nuisance/non-native plants from marsh platforms, and resulted in improved water quality for the bay due to enhanced stormwater treatment capacity of the pond.
Restoration_Technique: process-based physical restoration, species control, planting
Lead_Implementer: Southwest Florida Water Management District-S.W.I.M. Program

Project_Name: Myakka River State Park Vegetation Management
Project_Description: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission's (FWC) Aquatic Habitat Conservation and Restoration Section funded aerial herbicide treatments of exotic plant species in floodplain marsh habitats and wetlands within Myakka River State Park. Exotic plant targets were paragrass (Urochloa mutica) and West Indian marsh grass (Hymenachne amplexicaulis). The purpose of this project is to improve native plant diversity, wildlife foraging opportunities, water quality, and recreational access through a combination of aerial herbicide treatment and prescribed fire management in aquatic/wetlands areas of the park populated with dense, monotypic, non-native invasive vegetation. Aerial treatments were conducted on 10/3/2023 and 10/4/2023.

Project_Name: Myakka River State Park Vegetation Management
Project_Description: Vegetation management was conducted to improve habitat conditions for juvenile fish, wading birds, waterfowl and listed wildlife species that use the park. The removal of the seed source of these unwanted plants will also reduce the potential of spreading them further downstream. Paragrass and West Indian Marsh Grass both grow in thick mats that can impede water flow and restrict navigation, therefore these species were removed in order to increase water flow and allow for better navigation of the river. Peruvian Primrose Willow was also found within the floodplain marsh and in wetlands throughout the park; treatment and removal was conducted to allow the re-establishment of native vegetation.

Project_Description:
This project partially supplemented the natural sediment budget for the Perdido Key Unit of Gulf Islands National Seashore by placing at least 400,000 cubic yards (cy) of sediment dredged from Pensacola Pass onto the Gulfside eastern half of Perdido Key. The National Park Service (NPS) worked in close coordination with U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) to do so.

Project_Description: This effort was the first pilot project implemented as part of the larger Port Orange Shoreline Management Plan.  This project implemented a combination of living shoreline restoration techniques in a highly urbanized system to demonstrate the different shoreline stabilization techniques available for use in lieu of more traditional hardened shorelines.  With the permission of 16 homeowners the project was able to restore 0.5 acres of shoreline habitat composed of upland, saltmarsh, and oyster reef habitat. With the help of the project partners and 279 volunteers invasive species were removed, upland habitats were stabilized, Spartina was planted, and a variety of oyster restoration techniques were deployed.  Lessons learned from this project will be incorporated into future restoration efforts associated with the Port Orange Shoreline Management Plan.

Project_Name: Restoring Mangrove Islands in Pine Island Sound
Project_Description: This project restored mangrove and oyster reef habitat for fish and wildlife Species of Greatest Conservation Need in Pine Island Sound using methods demonstrated to work effectively in the area. Pine Island Sound is characterized by extensive mangrove shorelines and mangrove islands, fringing oyster reefs, and shallow seagrass beds which serve as important feeding, breeding, and nursery habitats for fish and wildlife. Repeated hurricanes and sea level rise damaged and degraded habitats on and surrounding five islands managed by the U. S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) as part of the Pine Island National Wildlife Refuge: Hemp Key, Bird Key, Benedict Key, Rat Key, and Cat Key. Restoration of resiliency and habitat function at these five islands is being achieved through planting of mangrove propagules, enhancement of oyster reefs, and structural and functional monitoring during this three-year project. Hemp Key is designated by FWC as a Critical Wildlife  Area because it supports a high density of nesting wading and diving birds. Pilot mangrove planting, oyster reef restoration, and initial monitoring were completed by Sanibel- Captiva Conservation Foundation (SCCF) staff and volunteers supported by a State Wildlife Grant (SWG) through USFWS. AHCR provided appropriation funding that was used deliver and stage 50 cubic yards of large fossil shell that was used in oyster reef enhancement. During subsequent grant years SCCF will continue mangrove and oyster restoration and monitoring.
Funding_Program: US Fish and Wildlife Service State Wildlife Grant Program (USFWS SWG)

Project_Description: The purpose of the "Smokehouse Bay Preserve Restoration" project is to restore hydrology and native vegetation within the Smokehouse Bay Preserve, a Lee County Conservation 2020 parcel located in Lee County on northern Pine Island, adjacent to Matlacha Pass. This project will restore hydrology and native vegetation on 51 of those preserve’s 268 acres. The western portion of the preserve consists of an abandoned palm grove which slopes to mangrove swamp and Smokehouse Bay. Non-indigenous invasive vegetation occurs both in the abandoned grove and within the adjacent mangrove swamp. The three phases of the project are: re-grading of the ditches and furrows to a more natural slope, treating non-indigenous invasive vegetation scattered throughout the abandoned palm grove, and planting of native plants (based on soil and historic aerials). Additional exotic plant treatments will continue over time, both on the abandoned palm grove and the mangrove swamp to the east.

Project_Description:
The Lake Worth Lagoon estuary in Palm Beach County (PBC) runs approximately 20 miles parallel to the southeast coastline of Florida. It is an urban estuary that has suffered extensive loss of estuarine habitats and degraded water quality due to human development activities over the past century. Approximately 81% of the lagoon’s shoreline is developed with seawalls associated with private residences and businesses. Dredge activities associated with development decades ago resulted in large benthic “holes” that now impair the Lagoon’s ecosystem. These “dredge holes” are typically well below grade, often anoxic, and generally do not support seagrass or wildlife. Additionally, canals that drain into the Lagoon have introduced fine, silty sediments that settle in these holes, hindering recruitment of seagrasses and diminishing water quality. The Tarpon Cove project will expand restoration efforts by filling in a deep dredge hole to restore and enhance important shallow estuarine seagrass habitat through the capping of anoxic, fine-grained organic sediments (i.e., muck). Capping the muck, by filling the hole, will allow for the natural recruitment of seagrasses, including Johnson’s seagrass (Halophila johnsonii), a federally threatened species, to naturally recruit. Additionally, the project will result in five intertidal islands consisting of mangrove, tidal saltmarsh, intertidal sand flat, and oyster reef habitats, along with a beach- nesting bird island. These islands are expected to support over 120 species of fish, 39 species of birds, and 14 state and/or federally listed species including West Indian manatee, Johnson’s sea grass, American oystercatcher and least tern. Other benefits of the project include downstream water-quality improvements, improved wildlife- and fisheries oriented recreational opportunities, increased protection of shorelines from coastal storms and flooding, and increased carbon sequestration capabilities, the latter of which contribute to resilience to the effects of climate change.
The final project, including all phases, will ultimately provide almost 40 acres of restored estuarine habitat.
Funding_Program: National Coastal Wetlands Conservation Grant Program (NCWCGP)
Partners: Palm Beach County Department of Environmental Resources Management (PBC ERM), Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP), National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), USFWS State Wildlife Grant Program (SWG)

Project_Description: This project restored the degraded saltmarsh and mangrove systems of Wildcat Cove Preserve within St. Lucie County, Florida.  This 129-acre site was impounded in the 1960’s for mosquito control purposes.  The Wildcat Cove restoration project reconnected the site to the Indian River Lagoon by removing invasive vegetation and installing six culverts.  This on-the-ground restoration project benefits living marine resources by increasing available habitat that is important to the refuge, spawning, and rearing areas essential to fisheries.  Not only did this project help to stabilize this estuarine system, but it also educated and engaged the local community through native species planting events and educational signage placed throughout the preserve. Approximately 99 acres of saltmarsh and mangrove habitat was restored.

Project_Description: This is an acquisition project for habitat protection and restoration and public access to restore mesic pine flatwoods, tidal wetlands and mangroves and create nature based, low impact educational and recreational opportunities.
Habitat_Description: This project includes acquisition of the 80 acre Wildflower Golf Club by the Lemon Bay Conservancy to be restored to natural conditions and used as a nature park. The current habitats in the preserve include mangroves and tidal creek, plus extensive grass areas with invasive salt bush, Spanish needles, dog fennel and invasive exotic Brazilian pepper. Lemon Creek flows through the parcel, connecting a series of ponds, all of which are tidally influenced. Historically, the parcel had hydric pine/palmetto flatwoods and inland scrub in addition to coastal mangroves. The habitats currently support a variety of wildlife species including legless island glass lizards, soldier butterfly, little blue herons, common moorhens, eagles, black crown night heron, blue crabs, juvenile tarpon. The acquisition, restoration planning and completion are accomplished by the non-profit Lemon Bay Conservancy and volunteers.
